### Install Actionflow via Bundler

Source: https://github.com/ljuti/actionflow

Add Actionflow to your Gemfile and run bundle install. The gem has zero runtime dependencies and requires Ruby >= 3.2.

```ruby
gem "actionflow"
```

--------------------------------

### Install Actionflow via RubyGems

Source: https://github.com/ljuti/actionflow

Install the gem directly. Then require it in your application to load the `Workflow` namespace.

```bash
gem install actionflow
```

```ruby
require "actionflow"
```

--------------------------------

### Define an Action with Expects and Promises

Source: https://github.com/ljuti/actionflow/blob/main/docs/developer-guide.md

Actions are ordinary Ruby objects that include `Workflow::Action`. Declare `expects` for keys the context must contain and `promises` for keys the action will produce. The framework verifies the contract at runtime — missing expected keys raise `Workflow::ExpectedKeysMissing`, missing promised keys raise `Workflow::PromisedKeysMissing`.

```ruby
class ChargeCard
  include Workflow::Action

  expects :user, :amount
  promises :charge

  def initialize(payment_gateway:)
    @payment_gateway = payment_gateway
  end

  def call(ctx)
    ctx[:charge] = @payment_gateway.charge(ctx[:user], ctx[:amount])
  end
end
```

--------------------------------

### Define Actions with Default Values

Source: https://github.com/ljuti/actionflow/blob/main/docs/developer-guide.md

Use `expects` with `default:` to provide static or callable defaults. Callable defaults receive the context and are evaluated when the key is missing. Defaults are applied before expected-key verification.

```ruby
class ApplyPromoCode
  include Workflow::Action

  expects :amount
  expects :promo_rate, default: 0.0
  expects :customer_tier, default: ->(ctx) { :standard }
  promises :adjusted_total

  def call(ctx)
    ctx[:adjusted_total] = (ctx[:amount] * (1 - ctx[:promo_rate])).round(2)
  end
end
```

--------------------------------

### Define Actions with Instance-Specific Contracts

Source: https://github.com/ljuti/actionflow/blob/main/docs/developer-guide.md

Override `#workflow_metadata` on the instance to build contracts from constructor arguments. This is useful for generic, reusable actions whose expected and promised keys vary per instance.

```ruby
class NormalizeField
  include Workflow::Action

  def initialize(from:, to:)
    @from = from
    @to = to
  end

  def workflow_metadata
    @metadata ||= Workflow::ActionMetadata.new(
      expected_keys: [@from],
      promised_keys: [@to]
    )
  end

  def call(ctx)
    ctx[@to] = ctx[@from].to_s.strip.downcase
  end
end

normalizer = NormalizeField.new(from: :name, to: :normalized_name)
```

--------------------------------

### Compose Actions with an Organizer

Source: https://github.com/ljuti/actionflow/blob/main/docs/developer-guide.md

Organizers compose action objects into a workflow. Include `Workflow::Organizer`, inject action instances through the constructor, and use `with(data).reduce(steps)` to execute. Organizers are plain objects — dependencies go in the constructor, business data goes in the context.

```ruby
class Checkout
  include Workflow::Organizer

  def initialize(validate_cart:, charge_card:, send_receipt:)
    @validate_cart = validate_cart
    @charge_card = charge_card
    @send_receipt = send_receipt
  end

  def call(cart:, user:, amount:)
    with(cart: cart, user: user, amount: amount).reduce(
      @validate_cart,
      @charge_card,
      @send_receipt
    )
  end
end
```

--------------------------------

### Run a Workflow and Check Results

Source: https://github.com/ljuti/actionflow/blob/main/docs/developer-guide.md

Instantiate the organizer with real dependencies and call it with business data. The returned context supports `success?`, `failure?`, `message`, `error_code`, bracket access for data, and `to_h` for a shallow copy.

```ruby
checkout = Checkout.new(
  validate_cart: ValidateCart.new,
  charge_card: ChargeCard.new(payment_gateway: StripeGateway.new),
  send_receipt: SendReceipt.new(mailer: ReceiptMailer)
)

result = checkout.call(cart: cart, user: user, amount: 100)

if result.success?
  puts result[:charge]
else
  puts result.message
  puts result.error_code
end
```

--------------------------------

### Handle Failure with fail!

Source: https://github.com/ljuti/actionflow/blob/main/docs/developer-guide.md

Call `ctx.fail!(message, error_code:)` inside an action to stop the pipeline and mark the context as failed. Remaining actions are not executed. The context remains in a failed state (`failure?` returns `true`).

```ruby
class ValidateOrder
  include Workflow::Action

  expects :order

  def call(ctx)
    if ctx[:order][:total] <= 0
      ctx.fail!("Order total must be positive", error_code: :invalid_order)
    else
      ctx[:valid] = true
    end
  end
end
```

--------------------------------

### Implement Rollback with fail_with_rollback!

Source: https://github.com/ljuti/actionflow/blob/main/docs/developer-guide.md

Define `#rollback(ctx)` on actions for compensation logic. When an action calls `ctx.fail_with_rollback!`, the framework runs rollback on all previously executed steps in reverse order. Rollback methods should guard against missing keys with `ctx.key?`.

```ruby
class ChargeCard
  include Workflow::Action

  expects :user, :amount
  promises :charge

  def initialize(payment_gateway:)
    @payment_gateway = payment_gateway
  end

  def call(ctx)
    ctx[:charge] = @payment_gateway.charge(ctx[:user], ctx[:amount])
  end

  def rollback(ctx)
    @payment_gateway.refund(ctx[:charge]) if ctx.key?(:charge)
  end
end

class AuditStep
  include Workflow::Action

  expects :charge

  def call(ctx)
    ctx.fail_with_rollback!("Compliance check failed")
  end
end
```

--------------------------------

### Skip Remaining Actions

Source: https://github.com/ljuti/actionflow/blob/main/docs/developer-guide.md

Use `ctx.skip_remaining!` to bail out of the current scope without marking failure, or `ctx.skip_all_remaining!` to skip all nested scopes. The context stays successful (`success?` remains `true`) but `stop_processing?` returns `true`.

```ruby
class ConditionalSkip
  include Workflow::Action

  expects :items

  def call(ctx)
    if ctx[:items].empty?
      ctx.skip_remaining!("No items to process")
    else
      ctx[:processed] = true
    end
  end
end
```

--------------------------------

### Use Conditional Execution with ReduceIf

Source: https://github.com/ljuti/actionflow/blob/main/docs/developer-guide.md

Run steps only when a condition lambda evaluates to true. The condition receives the context. Available as both a direct class and an organizer convenience method.

```ruby
class MyPipeline
  include Workflow::Organizer

  def call(order:, notify: false)
    with(order: order, notify: notify).reduce(
      ValidateOrder.new,
      reduce_if(->(ctx) { ctx[:notify] }, [
        SendNotification.new
      ])
    )
  end
end
```

--------------------------------

### Branch with ReduceIfElse

Source: https://github.com/ljuti/actionflow/blob/main/docs/developer-guide.md

Execute one of two step arrays based on a condition. Both branches receive the same context.

```ruby
class TieredDiscount
  include Workflow::Organizer

  def initialize
    @gold_discount = ApplyGoldDiscount.new
    @standard_discount = ApplyStandardDiscount.new
  end

  def call(order:, tier:)
    with(order: order, tier: tier).reduce(
      Workflow::Steps::ReduceIfElse.new(
        ->(ctx) { ctx[:tier] == :gold },
        [@gold_discount],
        [@standard_discount]
      )
    )
  end
end
```

--------------------------------

### Iterate Over Collections

Source: https://github.com/ljuti/actionflow/blob/main/docs/developer-guide.md

Run steps for each item in a collection. The current item is placed in the context under a key derived from the collection name (e.g., `:items` becomes `:item`). Override with `item_key:`.

```ruby
class ProcessAllItems
  include Workflow::Organizer

  def initialize
    @process = ProcessItem.new
  end

  def call(items:)
    with(items: items).reduce(
      iterate(:items, [@process])
    )
  end
end

# With explicit item key
iterate(:orders, [ProcessOrder.new], item_key: :order)
```

--------------------------------

### Loop with ReduceWhile and ReduceUntil

Source: https://github.com/ljuti/actionflow/blob/main/docs/developer-guide.md

`ReduceWhile` loops while a condition is true. `ReduceUntil` loops until a condition is true. Both break early if the context is stopped (failure or skip).

```ruby
# Retry while attempts remain
Workflow::Steps::ReduceWhile.new(
  ->(ctx) { ctx[:attempts] < 3 },
  [RetryWithBackoff.new]
)

# Refine until converged
Workflow::Steps::ReduceUntil.new(
  ->(ctx) { ctx[:converged] == true },
  [RefineEstimate.new]
)
```

--------------------------------

### Branch on a Value with ReduceCase

Source: https://github.com/ljuti/actionflow/blob/main/docs/developer-guide.md

Branch on a value extracted from the context, similar to a switch statement. The value function receives the context. Each branch is an array of steps.

```ruby
Workflow::Steps::ReduceCase.new(
  ->(ctx) { ctx[:role] },
  {
    admin: [LoadAdminDashboard.new],
    editor: [LoadEditorDashboard.new],
    viewer: [LoadViewerDashboard.new]
  }
)
```

--------------------------------

### Inject Data and Aliases into Context

Source: https://github.com/ljuti/actionflow/blob/main/docs/developer-guide.md

`AddToContext` injects key-value pairs. `AddAliases` registers key aliases so that `ctx[:alias]` resolves to `ctx[:original]`. Both are useful as inline steps without defining a full action class.

```ruby
# Inject static values
Workflow::Steps::AddToContext.new(status: "pending", retry_count: 0)

# Register aliases
Workflow::Steps::AddAliases.new(name: :full_name)
# After this: ctx[:name] resolves to ctx[:full_name]
```

--------------------------------

### Execute Inline Blocks

Source: https://github.com/ljuti/actionflow/blob/main/docs/developer-guide.md

Wrap an inline block as a step. Useful for quick transformations that don't warrant a full action class. Available as both a direct class and an organizer convenience method.

```ruby
# Using organizer convenience method
with(data).reduce(
  execute { |ctx| ctx[:timestamp] = Time.now.utc.to_i; ctx },
  ProcessData.new
)

# Using step class directly
Workflow::Steps::Execute.new(->(ctx) { ctx[:stamp] = Time.now.utc.to_i; ctx })
```

--------------------------------

### Defer Work with WithCallback

Source: https://github.com/ljuti/actionflow/blob/main/docs/developer-guide.md

Run immediate steps, then store a callback for later invocation. The callback is a proc stored in the context under the given key. Call it later with `ctx[:key].call(ctx)`.

```ruby
Workflow::Steps::WithCallback.new(
  :on_complete,
  [PrepareData.new],     # run immediately
  [SendNotification.new] # stored as callback
)

# Later:
ctx[:on_complete].call(ctx)
```

--------------------------------

### Register Hooks on a Workflow

Source: https://github.com/ljuti/actionflow/blob/main/docs/developer-guide.md

Register `before_each`, `after_each`, and `around_each` hooks on the session returned by `with`. Hooks fire for each workflow action (objects with `workflow_metadata`), not for plain lambdas or control-flow steps. Around hooks must call `yield` to continue.

```ruby
class MyPipeline
  include Workflow::Organizer

  def call(data:)
    with(data)
      .before_each(->(action, ctx) { logger.info("Before #{action.class.name}") })
      .after_each(->(action, ctx) { logger.info("After #{action.class.name}") })
      .reduce(step_a, step_b)
  end
end
```

--------------------------------

### Measure Duration with Around Hooks

Source: https://github.com/ljuti/actionflow/blob/main/docs/developer-guide.md

Around hooks wrap action execution. They receive the action, context, and a block. Multiple around hooks compose naturally — outer wraps inner wraps action. Use `&blk` parameter or `yield` to continue the chain.

```ruby
class LogDuration
  def initialize(logger:)
    @logger = logger
  end

  def call(action, ctx)
    start = Process.clock_gettime(Process::CLOCK_MONOTONIC)
    result = yield
    elapsed = Process.clock_gettime(Process::CLOCK_MONOTONIC) - start
    @logger.info(action: action.class.name, duration_ms: (elapsed * 1000).round(2))
    result
  end
end

with(data)
  .around_each(LogDuration.new(logger: logger))
  .reduce(steps)
```

--------------------------------

### Configure Actionflow Globally

Source: https://github.com/ljuti/actionflow/blob/main/docs/developer-guide.md

Use `Workflow.configure` to set global options. Available settings: `logger` (for framework logging), `localization_adapter` (for translating failure messages), and `strict_context_access` (raise on undefined dynamic accessors).

```ruby
Workflow.configure do |config|
  config.logger = Logger.new($stdout)
  config.localization_adapter = Workflow::Localization::HashAdapter.new(catalog)
  config.strict_context_access = false
end
```

--------------------------------

### Localize Failure Messages with HashAdapter

Source: https://github.com/ljuti/actionflow/blob/main/docs/developer-guide.md

Configure a localization adapter to translate `fail!` message keys. `HashAdapter` looks up messages in a hash catalog and falls back to the raw message for unknown keys. `NullAdapter` returns messages unchanged (default behavior when no adapter is set).

```ruby
catalog = {
  "charge_card.card_declined" => "Your card was declined. Please try another payment method.",
  "charge_card.gateway_timeout" => "Payment processing timed out. Please try again."
}

Workflow.configure do |config|
  config.localization_adapter = Workflow::Localization::HashAdapter.new(catalog)
end

# In an action:
ctx.fail!("charge_card.card_declined")
# result.message => "Your card was declined. Please try another payment method."
```

--------------------------------

### Test Actions in Isolation

Source: https://github.com/ljuti/actionflow/blob/main/docs/developer-guide.md

Use `#execute(ctx)` to run through the full lifecycle (contract checks, defaults, hooks). Use `#call(ctx)` to bypass the framework and test only raw business logic. Both return the context.

```ruby
# Full lifecycle (recommended for most tests)
action = ChargeCard.new(payment_gateway: fake_gateway)
result = action.execute(Workflow::Context.new(user: user, amount: 100))
expect(result).to be_success
expect(result[:charge]).to be_present

# Business logic only (faster, no contract enforcement)
action = ChargeCard.new(payment_gateway: fake_gateway)
ctx = Workflow::Context.new(user: user, amount: 100)
action.call(ctx)
expect(ctx[:charge]).to be_present
```

--------------------------------

### Test Organizers End-to-End

Source: https://github.com/ljuti/actionflow/blob/main/docs/developer-guide.md

Inject fake dependencies into the organizer and call it with test data. Assert on the returned context's success status, error codes, and data.

```ruby
checkout = Checkout.new(
  validate_cart: ValidateCart.new,
  charge_card: ChargeCard.new(payment_gateway: fake_gateway),
  send_receipt: SendReceipt.new(mailer: fake_mailer)
)

result = checkout.call(cart: cart, user: user, amount: 100)

expect(result).to be_success
expect(result[:charge]).to be_present
```

--------------------------------

### Build Test Context with ContextFactory

Source: https://github.com/ljuti/actionflow/blob/main/docs/developer-guide.md

Use `Workflow::Testing::ContextFactory` to build the context as it would appear just before a specific action runs. Look up by instance or by class. Override specific values with `with(...)` — overrides take precedence over step outputs.

```ruby
ctx = Workflow::Testing::ContextFactory
  .make_from(pipeline)
  .before(ApplyDiscount.new)   # or .before(ApplyDiscount) by class
  .with(product_id: "p1", discount_percent: 0.5)

# ctx has :product populated by preceding steps
# :discount_percent is overridden to 0.5

result = ApplyDiscount.new.execute(ctx)
expect(result[:final_price]).to eq(50.0)
```

--------------------------------

### Handle Contract Violations

Source: https://github.com/ljuti/actionflow/blob/main/docs/developer-guide.md

The framework raises two exception types for contract violations. `Workflow::ExpectedKeysMissing` when required keys are absent before `#call`. `Workflow::PromisedKeysMissing` when promised keys are absent after `#call` on a successful context. Promised keys are not checked on failed contexts.

```ruby
# Missing expected key
begin
  CalculateDiscount.new.execute(Workflow::Context.new(amount: 100))
rescue Workflow::ExpectedKeysMissing => e
  puts e.message  # "Missing expected keys: [:tier]"
end

# Missing promised key
begin
  action.execute(Workflow::Context.new(x: 1))
rescue Workflow::PromisedKeysMissing => e
  puts e.message  # "Missing promised keys: [:y]"
end
```

--------------------------------

### Context Data Access

Source: https://github.com/ljuti/actionflow/blob/main/docs/developer-guide.md

Context wraps a hash with symbolized keys. Use bracket notation for all reads and writes. It tracks success/failure state, skip flags, message, and error code. Aliases allow key remapping so `ctx[:alias]` resolves to `ctx[:original]`.

```APIDOC
## Workflow::Context Data Access

### Methods
- `ctx[:key]` — read a value
- `ctx[:key] = value` — write a value
- `ctx.key?(:key)` — check existence
- `ctx.keys` — array of symbol keys
- `ctx.to_h` — shallow copy of the underlying hash
- `ctx.success?` / `ctx.failure?` — pipeline status
- `ctx.message` — failure or skip message
- `ctx.error_code` — structured error identifier
- `ctx.stop_processing?` — true if failed or skipped

### Usage

```ruby
ctx = Workflow::Context.new(order_id: "ord_123")
ctx[:total] = 99.95

ctx[:total]           # 99.95
ctx.key?(:total)      # true
ctx.keys              # [:order_id, :total]
ctx.success?          # true
ctx.message           # nil
```
```

--------------------------------

### Register AI Capabilities

Source: https://github.com/ljuti/actionflow/blob/main/docs/developer-guide.md

Wrap actions with `Workflow::Ai::Capability` to expose metadata safe for AI agents. Capabilities carry `expects`, `promises`, `side_effects`, `risk` level, and approval requirements. Register them in a `CapabilityRegistry`. Use `to_description` to get a hash without the action reference.

```ruby
registry = Workflow::Ai::CapabilityRegistry.new

registry.register(Workflow::Ai::Capability.new(
  :find_order,
  action: FindOrder.new(order_repository: repo),
  description: "Finds an order by order_id.",
  expects: [:order_id],
  promises: [:order],
  side_effects: [],
  risk: :low
))

registry.register(Workflow::Ai::Capability.new(
  :issue_refund,
  action: IssueRefund.new(payment_gateway: gateway),
  description: "Issues a refund for a validated order.",
  expects: [:order, :valid],
  promises: [:refund_id],
  side_effects: [:payment_refund],
  risk: :high,
  requires_approval: true
))

registry.descriptions  # array of sanitized hashes for agent consumption
```

--------------------------------

### Validate an AI-Generated Plan

Source: https://github.com/ljuti/actionflow/blob/main/docs/developer-guide.md

`PlanValidator` simulates key flow without executing actions. It checks that all step IDs are registered and that all expected keys are available at each step. Returns a `ValidationResult` with `safe?`, `errors`, and `requires_approval?`.

```ruby
plan = Workflow::Ai::Plan.new({
  "name" => "refund_order",
  "steps" => [
    {"id" => "find_order"},
    {"id" => "validate_order"},
    {"id" => "issue_refund"}
  ]
})

validator = Workflow::Ai::PlanValidator.new(registry: registry)
result = validator.validate(plan, initial_keys: [:order_id])

result.safe?               # true / false
result.errors              # array of error strings
result.requires_approval?  # true if any high-risk step is included
```

--------------------------------

### Compile and Execute an AI Plan

Source: https://github.com/ljuti/actionflow/blob/main/docs/developer-guide.md

`PlanCompiler` turns a validated plan into executable step objects. Linear steps resolve to action objects, conditionals to `ReduceIfElse`, iterations to `Iterate`. `DynamicOrganizer` executes compiled plans using the standard runtime.

```ruby
compiler = Workflow::Ai::PlanCompiler.new(registry: registry)
steps = compiler.compile(plan)

organizer = Workflow::Ai::DynamicOrganizer.new(
  steps: steps,
  before_hooks: [AuditHook.new]
)

result = organizer.call(order_id: "ord_123")

result.success?  # => true
result[:order]   # => {id: "ord_123", ...}
result[:refund_id]
```

--------------------------------

### Compose Nested Control Flow

Source: https://github.com/ljuti/actionflow/blob/main/docs/developer-guide.md

All control-flow steps compose naturally inside an organizer. ReduceIf, Iterate, ReduceIfElse, and other steps can be nested to express complex workflows. Use organizer convenience methods (`reduce_if`, `iterate`, `execute`) or step classes directly.

```ruby
class OrderPipeline
  include Workflow::Organizer

  def initialize
    @fetch = FetchItems.new
    @process_urgent = ProcessUrgent.new
    @process_normal = ProcessNormal.new
    @notify_empty = NotifyEmpty.new
  end

  def call(data)
    with(data).reduce(
      @fetch,
      reduce_if(->(ctx) { ctx[:items].empty? }, [
        @notify_empty
      ]),
      iterate(:items, [
        Workflow::Steps::ReduceIfElse.new(
          ->(ctx) { ctx[:item][:urgent] },
          [@process_urgent],
          [@process_normal]
        )
      ])
    )
  end
end
```

--------------------------------

### Action Lifecycle and Execution Model

Source: https://github.com/ljuti/actionflow/blob/main/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md

When an organizer calls `reduce`, the Reducer iterates over steps. For workflow actions (objects responding to `workflow_metadata`), the `ActionRunner` applies defaults, verifies expected keys, runs before hooks, runs around hooks (wrapping `action.call(ctx)`), verifies promised keys on success, then runs after hooks. Control-flow steps and plain callables are invoked directly via `step.call(ctx)`.

```APIDOC
## Action Execution Lifecycle

### Per-step execution order
1. `ctx.stop_processing?` check — skip if already failed/skipped
2. `ctx.current_step = action` — set current step reference
3. Apply defaults for missing expected keys
4. Verify all expected keys present (raise `ExpectedKeysMissing`)
5. Run `before_each` hooks
6. Run `around_each` hooks (wrapping `action.call(ctx)`)
7. Verify promised keys present if context is successful (raise `PromisedKeysMissing`)
8. Run `after_each` hooks

### Methods
- `action.execute(ctx)` — full lifecycle (use in tests)
- `action.call(ctx)` — raw business logic only
- `ctx.stop_processing?` — checked before each step in the reducer

### Key invariants
- Dependencies (services, gateways) go in the action constructor, never in the context
- Business data flows through the context via `ctx[:key]` bracket notation
- The pipeline calls `#execute`, not `#call` — `#call` is the raw business method
- Hooks fire only for workflow actions, not for plain lambdas or control-flow steps
```

--------------------------------

### Actionflow Error Reference

Source: https://github.com/ljuti/actionflow/blob/main/docs/developer-guide.md

The gem defines three error classes under the `Workflow` namespace. `ExpectedKeysMissing` and `PromisedKeysMissing` are raised by the ActionRunner during contract enforcement. `FailWithRollback` is raised internally by `ctx.fail_with_rollback!` and caught by the Reducer to trigger reverse-order rollback.

```APIDOC
## Error Reference

### Workflow::ExpectedKeysMissing
Raised when an action's `expects` keys are not present in the context before `#call` runs.

### Workflow::PromisedKeysMissing
Raised when an action's `promises` keys are not set after `#call` on a successful context. Not raised when the context has failed.

### Workflow::FailWithRollback
Raised internally by `ctx.fail_with_rollback!`. The Reducer catches this exception and runs `#rollback(ctx)` on all previously executed steps in reverse order.
```

--------------------------------

### Actionflow Namespace and Module Structure

Source: https://github.com/ljuti/actionflow/blob/main/docs/developer-guide.md

All functionality lives under the `Workflow` namespace. The gem is required as `require "actionflow"`. Core types are autoloaded. Optional modules (`Ai`, `Testing`) are available but not required for basic usage.

```APIDOC
## Namespace Structure

### Core (always available)
- `Workflow::Context` — data carrier with success/failure/skip tracking
- `Workflow::Action` — module to include in action classes
- `Workflow::ActionMetadata` — stores expects/promises/defaults
- `Workflow::ActionRunner` — executes the full action lifecycle
- `Workflow::Organizer` — module to include in organizer classes
- `Workflow::OrganizerSession` — accumulates hooks, runs reduce
- `Workflow::Reducer` — iterates steps, handles rollback
- `Workflow::RollbackStrategy` — runs rollback in reverse order
- `Workflow::Configuration` — singleton config (logger, localization)
- `Workflow::Localization` — NullAdapter and HashAdapter

### Control-Flow Steps (Workflow::Steps)
- `ReduceIf` — conditional execution
- `ReduceIfElse` — conditional branching
- `ReduceWhile` — loop while true
- `ReduceUntil` — loop until true
- `ReduceCase` — switch on a value
- `Iterate` — loop over a collection
- `Execute` — inline block
- `AddToContext` — inject key-value pairs
- `AddAliases` — register key aliases
- `WithCallback` — defer work for later

### AI Module (Workflow::Ai — optional)
- `Capability` — action wrapper with agent-safe metadata
- `CapabilityRegistry` — register and look up capabilities
- `Plan` — structured workflow plan from an agent
- `PlanValidator` — simulate key flow, check safety
- `PlanCompiler` — compile plan into executable steps
- `DynamicOrganizer` — execute compiled plans

### Testing (Workflow::Testing)
- `ContextFactory` — build context as it appears before a target action

### Errors
- `Workflow::ExpectedKeysMissing`
- `Workflow::PromisedKeysMissing`
- `Workflow::FailWithRollback`
```

--------------------------------

### Full Example: E-Commerce Checkout with Rollback

Source: https://github.com/ljuti/actionflow/blob/main/examples/03_failure_and_rollback.rb

A complete example showing a multi-step checkout workflow with rollback support. Each action defines `#rollback(ctx)` for compensation. The `AuditCompliance` action demonstrates `fail_with_rollback!` which triggers reverse-order rollback of all previously executed steps.

```ruby
class PlaceOrder
  include Workflow::Organizer

  def initialize(inventory:, gateway:, shipping:, audit:)
    @reserve = ReserveInventory.new(inventory: inventory)
    @charge = ChargePayment.new(gateway: gateway)
    @ship = ShipOrder.new(shipping: shipping)
    @audit = AuditCompliance.new(audit_service: audit)
  end

  def call(user:, item_id:, quantity:, amount:)
    with(user: user, item_id: item_id, quantity: quantity, amount: amount)
      .reduce(@reserve, @charge, @audit, @ship)
  end
end

result = PlaceOrder.new(inventory: inv, gateway: gw, shipping: shp, audit: aud)
  .call(user: "alice", item_id: "sku-1", quantity: 2, amount: 49.99)

result.success?           # true on success
result[:reservation]      # set by ReserveInventory
result[:charge_id]        # set by ChargePayment
result[:tracking_number]  # set by ShipOrder
```
